claims.text: Initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention reduces net cardiovascular harm in adults aged 60 and over.
Initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention increases net cardiovascular harm in adults aged 60 and over.
Initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention has no net effect on cardiovascular harm in adults aged 60 and over.
For adults aged 60 and over, whether initiating aspirin reduces net cardiovascular harm depends on how sources define and value cardiovascular events and bleeding complications.

For adults aged 60 and over, interpreting net cardiovascular harm to include major extracranial bleeding makes aspirin initiation less favorable than an interpretation restricted to cardiovascular outcomes.

For adults aged 60 and over, severity-sensitive interpretations of net cardiovascular harm can give a different balance for aspirin initiation than comparisons that do not distinguish outcome severity.
For adults aged 60 and over, differences in outcome inclusion and severity valuation do not change the net cardiovascular harm conclusion for aspirin initiation.
Net cardiovascular harm has no single accepted definition for aspirin primary prevention in adults aged 60 and over; sources use distinct outcomes and severity valuations.
Initiating low-dose aspirin reduces first myocardial infarction in adults aged 60 and older without established cardiovascular disease.
Initiating low-dose aspirin reduces ischemic stroke in adults aged 60 and older without established cardiovascular disease.
Initiating low-dose aspirin reduces cardiovascular death in adults aged 60 and older without established cardiovascular disease.
Initiating low-dose aspirin has no effect on first myocardial infarction, ischemic stroke, or cardiovascular death in adults aged 60 and older without established cardiovascular disease.
Initiating low-dose aspirin increases intracranial hemorrhage in adults aged 60 and older without established cardiovascular disease.
Initiating low-dose aspirin increases nonfatal major extracranial bleeding in adults aged 60 and older without established cardiovascular disease.
Initiating low-dose aspirin increases fatal bleeding in adults aged 60 and older without established cardiovascular disease.
Among adults aged 60 and older without established cardiovascular disease, aspirin initiation causes a larger absolute excess of major bleeding at older ages and higher baseline bleeding risk.
Initiating low-dose aspirin does not increase intracranial hemorrhage or major extracranial bleeding in adults aged 60 and older without established cardiovascular disease.
